Pattern 04 of 21

Fast & Slow Pointers

Send two runners down the same path, one twice as fast as the other. Where and whether they meet tells you about the shape of the path (its middle, whether it loops, and where the loop begins) using O(1) memory.

1. What is this pattern for?

A tortoise and a hare race on a track. If the track is a straight road, the hare simply reaches the end first, and at that moment the tortoise is exactly halfway. If the track is a circular running loop, the hare eventually comes around from behind and laps the tortoise. They can only meet if there's a loop.

This pattern (also called Floyd's tortoise and hare) works on anything where "go to the next thing" is well defined: a linked list (node.next), an array used as a map (i → nums[i]), or a function (n → sum of squares of digits). It answers:

  • Is there a cycle? (they meet ⇔ yes)
  • Where does the cycle start? (a second, equal-speed walk)
  • Where's the middle? (when fast hits the end, slow is in the middle). That's the first step of many list problems: palindrome check, reorder, split for merge sort.

The alternative is a hash set of visited nodes, which needs O(n) memory. Fast & slow uses O(1).

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Start both at the head. slow = head and fast = head.
  2. Move at different speeds. Each round: slow = slow.next (1 step), fast = fast.next.next (2 steps). Guard with while fast and fast.next so fast never steps off the end.
  3. No cycle → fast falls off. When the loop ends, fast has walked twice as far, so slow is at the middle (the second middle for even lengths).
  4. Cycle → they meet. Inside the loop, the gap between them shrinks by exactly 1 every round, so fast can't jump over slow. They must land on the same node within one lap.
  5. Find the entrance. Put one pointer back at the head and move both 1 step at a time. They meet exactly at the cycle's first node. (Why: if the tail has length a and they met b steps into a loop of length L, then 2(a+b) = a+b+kL, so a = kL − b: walking a steps from the meeting point lands on the entrance.)

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot Fast & Slow

Trigger words

  • "linked list" + "cycle", "loop", "where the cycle begins"
  • "middle of the linked list", "second half", "palindrome linked list", "reorder"
  • "find the duplicate" with values in 1..n, "without modifying the array", "O(1) space"
  • "repeat the process… does it end in 1 or loop forever?" (Happy Number)
  • "circular array", "jump forward/backward by nums[i]"

Shape of the input

  • A next-function: node.next, nums[i], or a computed successor.
  • You can only walk forward (singly linked), and you don't know the length.
  • Brute-force smell: "store every visited node in a set" or "count the length first, then walk again". The interviewer then asks for O(1) space or one pass.
The one question to ask"Is there a 'next' rule I keep following, and do I care whether it loops or where its middle is?" If yes, race two pointers at speeds 1 and 2.

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use Fast & Slow when…Prefer something else when…
Detecting a cycle / its start in O(1) spaceMemory isn't a concern and you want simple code: a set() of visited nodes
Finding the middle of a singly linked list in one passYou have random access (an array): just use n // 2
Splitting a list before reversing half (palindrome, reorder)The task is to reverse a list or parts of it: that's LinkedList Reversal (often used right after this one)
Duplicate in 1..n without modifying the arrayThe pointers walk toward each other on a sorted array: that's Two Pointers
Cycle in an implicit "next" functionCycles in a general graph (many edges per node): use DFS with colours, or topological sort

Cost: O(n) time. Fast covers at most ~2n steps before falling off or meeting, and phase 2 is at most n more. O(1) extra space.

5. The Python template (memorize this)

# A) Middle of a list (the second middle when the length is even)
def middle_node(head):
    # Both runners start on the first node.
    slow = head
    fast = head
    # fast jumps 2 nodes per round, so BOTH fast and fast.next must exist.
    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
        slow = slow.next              # tortoise: 1 step
        fast = fast.next.next         # hare: 2 steps
    # fast has walked twice as far as slow, so slow is halfway.
    return slow


# B) Cycle detection
def has_cycle(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head
    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        # Compare NODES with "is", not values: two nodes may hold equal values.
        if slow is fast:
            return True               # the hare lapped the tortoise: a loop
    return False                      # the hare fell off the end: no loop


# C) Start of the cycle (LeetCode 142)
def cycle_start(head):
    slow = head
    fast = head
    while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
        slow = slow.next
        fast = fast.next.next
        if slow is fast:
            # Phase 1 is done: they met somewhere inside the loop.
            # Phase 2: send one runner back to the start ...
            slow = head
            # ... and move BOTH one step at a time until they meet again.
            while slow is not fast:
                slow = slow.next
                fast = fast.next
            return slow               # the node where they meet is the entrance
    return None                       # no loop, so no entrance

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. slow = head and fast = head: both runners start on the first node. (We write two separate lines instead of the shortcut slow = fast = head.)
  2. while fast is not None and fast.next is not None: the hare is about to take two steps, so the node it stands on and the node after it must both exist. The order matters: Python checks fast is not None first and stops right there if it is false, so fast.next is never read on None. This is the long way of writing while fast and fast.next.
  3. slow = slow.next moves the tortoise one node; fast = fast.next.next moves the hare two nodes.
  4. Template A just returns slow when the loop stops. The hare walked twice as far, so the tortoise is halfway.
  5. Template B adds if slow is fast: return True after moving. is asks "is this the very same node object?", which is what we want. Two different nodes can hold the same number. If the loop ends without a meeting, the hare found the end of the list, so we return False.
  6. Template C does the same as B, but when they meet it starts phase 2: slow = head puts one runner back at the start, and the inner while slow is not fast: moves both runners one step at a time. The node where they meet again is the first node of the loop.

Dry run on the example: Template A on 1 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 5 (values shown for each node), then template C on LeetCode 142's list 3 → 2 → 0 → -4 whose tail points back to the node 2.

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Hare laps tortoise"A straight road: the hare finishes while the tortoise is at halftime. A running track: the hare laps the tortoise. Then both stroll from (start, meeting point) and bump into each other at the gate.

Picture

The Greek letter ρ (rho): a tail leading into a loop. The meeting happens on the loop; the gate is where the tail joins it.

Chant

"One step, two steps. Meet? Loop. Reset one, walk both, meet at the gate."

Guard rule

"Check fast and fast.next." The fast runner looks two steps ahead before jumping.

7. LeetCode problems, solved step by step

Medium 287. Find the Duplicate Number Array

Problem: nums has n + 1 integers, each in 1..n. Exactly one value repeats (possibly many times). Find it without modifying the array and with O(1) extra space.

Spot it: values are valid indices, so treat i → nums[i] as a "next" pointer. Index 0 is never a target (values ≥ 1), so it's the head of a tail. Two indices point at the duplicate value, so that node has two arrows coming in: the entrance of a cycle. "Duplicate + O(1) space + read-only" means Floyd.

Key insight: the duplicate is the cycle start. Run template C with slow = nums[slow] and fast = nums[nums[fast]].

Approach:

  1. Treat each index i as a node whose next is nums[i], starting from index 0.
  2. Phase 1: slow = nums[slow], fast = nums[nums[fast]] until they're equal.
  3. Phase 2: reset slow to the start (nums[0]) and keep fast at the meeting point.
  4. Move both one hop at a time. Where they meet is the cycle entrance, which is the duplicate.
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def findDuplicate(self, nums: List[int]) -> int:
        # Treat every index as a "node" and nums[index] as its "next" arrow.
        # Index 0 is the head (no value is 0, so nothing points back at it).
        # One hop from index 0 lands on nums[0]; both runners start there.
        slow = nums[0]
        fast = nums[0]

        # Phase 1: slow hops once, fast hops twice, until they land together.
        while True:
            slow = nums[slow]          # slow: 1 hop
            fast = nums[fast]          # fast: first hop
            fast = nums[fast]          # fast: second hop (same as nums[nums[fast]])
            if slow == fast:
                break                  # they met somewhere inside the loop

        # Phase 2: put slow back at the start, leave fast at the meeting point.
        slow = nums[0]
        # Both now hop ONE step at a time; they meet at the loop entrance.
        while slow != fast:
            slow = nums[slow]
            fast = nums[fast]

        # Two different indices point at the entrance, so it is the duplicate.
        return slow

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. slow = nums[0] and fast = nums[0]: index 0 is the "head" of our hidden linked list (no value is 0, so no arrow ever points back to index 0). Its arrow leads to nums[0], so both runners start there.
  2. while True: we don't know how many rounds phase 1 needs, so we loop "forever" and leave with break.
  3. Inside the loop, slow = nums[slow] follows one arrow. fast = nums[fast] written twice follows two arrows. That is the same as nums[nums[fast]], split into two easy lines.
  4. if slow == fast: break: they are on the same index, so they met inside the loop. We compare after moving because they start out equal.
  5. Phase 2: slow = nums[0] sends slow back to the start while fast stays at the meeting point. while slow != fast: moves both one arrow at a time.
  6. return slow: where they meet is the entrance of the loop. Two different indices point to it, so that value appears twice: it is the duplicate.

Dry run on the example: nums = [1, 3, 4, 2, 2] (expected answer 2). The arrows are 0→1, 1→3, 2→4, 3→2, 4→2.

PhaseRoundslowfastWhat happened
1start11both start at nums[0] = 1
1132slow: nums[1] = 3; fast: nums[1] = 3, then nums[3] = 2
1222slow: nums[3] = 2; fast: nums[2] = 4, then nums[4] = 2 → equal, break
2reset12slow = nums[0] = 1, fast stays
2134not equal yet
2222equal → return 2

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 142. Linked List Cycle II Linked List

Problem: Return the node where the cycle begins, or None if the list has no cycle. Don't modify the list.

Spot it: "where the cycle begins" + linked list. It's template C exactly; the second visualizer above traces it.

Key insight: distance from head to entrance = distance from meeting point to entrance (mod the loop length).

Approach:

  1. Run Floyd: slow 1 step, fast 2 steps, until they meet or fast falls off (no cycle → None).
  2. Reset slow to head.
  3. Move slow and fast one step each until they're the same node.
  4. Return that node: the cycle's entrance.
class Solution:
    def detectCycle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Both runners start at the head of the list.
        slow = head
        fast = head

        # Phase 1: slow moves 1 step, fast moves 2 steps, until they meet
        # or fast runs off the end of the list.
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
            if slow is fast:
                # Same NODE: fast lapped slow, so the list has a cycle.
                # Phase 2: send slow back to the head, keep fast where they met.
                slow = head
                # Move both ONE step at a time; they meet at the entrance.
                while slow is not fast:
                    slow = slow.next
                    fast = fast.next
                return slow

        # fast reached the end of the list, so there is no cycle.
        return None

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. slow = head, fast = head: both runners start at the head.
  2. while fast is not None and fast.next is not None: keep going only while the hare can take two steps. If it can't, the list has an end, so there is no cycle.
  3. slow = slow.next (1 step) and fast = fast.next.next (2 steps).
  4. if slow is fast: both point at the same node object, so the hare has lapped the tortoise: there is a cycle.
  5. Phase 2: slow = head moves one runner back to the head; fast stays at the meeting point. The math in section 2 says both are now the same distance from the entrance.
  6. while slow is not fast: move both one step at a time. When they become the same node, return slow returns the entrance.
  7. return None after the outer loop: the hare fell off the end, so there is no cycle.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 1, head = [3, 2, 0, -4], pos = 1 (the tail -4 points back to the node 2). Node values are shown.

PhaseRoundslowfastWhat happened

1120different nodes
1202different nodes
13-4-4same node: they met
2reset3-4slow back to the head
2122same node: the entrance

The function returns the node with value 2 (index 1).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 143. Reorder List Linked List

Problem: Rearrange L0 → L1 → … → Ln into L0 → Ln → L1 → Ln−1 → … in place.

Spot it: you need the back half in reverse order. That's (1) find the middle with fast/slow, (2) reverse the second half (pattern 05), (3) weave.

Key insight: stop slow at the end of the first half (while fast.next and fast.next.next) so you can cut slow.next = None.

Approach:

  1. Find the end of the first half with fast/slow (loop while fast.next and fast.next.next).
  2. Cut the list after slow and reverse the second half.
  3. Weave: one node from the first half, then one from the reversed second half, and so on.
  4. The first half is equal or one longer, so stop when the second half runs out.
class Solution:
    def reorderList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> None:
        # A list with 0 or 1 nodes is already in the right order.
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return

        # Step 1: find the END of the first half.
        # Looking at fast.next and fast.next.next makes slow stop one node
        # earlier than usual: on the last node of the first half.
        slow = head
        fast = head
        while fast.next is not None and fast.next.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        # Step 2: cut the list after slow ...
        second_half = slow.next
        slow.next = None                          # the first half now ends at slow
        # ... and reverse the second half (pattern 05).
        previous_node = None
        current_node = second_half
        while current_node is not None:
            next_node = current_node.next         # remember the rest of the list
            current_node.next = previous_node     # flip this node's arrow backwards
            previous_node = current_node          # previous moves forward
            current_node = next_node              # current moves forward
        # previous_node is now the first node of the reversed second half.

        # Step 3: weave: one node from the first half, then one from the second.
        first = head
        second = previous_node
        while second is not None:
            first_next = first.next               # save the rest of the first half
            second_next = second.next             # save the rest of the second half
            first.next = second                   # first node points to second node
            second.next = first_next              # second node points to the next first-half node
            first = first_next                    # step forward in the first half
            second = second_next                  # step forward in the second half

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if head is None or head.next is None: return: an empty list or a single node is already in the right order.
  2. Step 1, find the end of the first half. Both runners start at head. The loop condition fast.next is not None and fast.next.next is not None looks one node further ahead than the usual check, so slow stops on the last node of the first half (the first middle).
  3. Step 2, cut. second_half = slow.next remembers where the second half begins. slow.next = None ends the first half there, so now we have two separate lists.
  4. Step 2, reverse the second half. previous_node starts as None and current_node at the start of the second half. Each loop round: save next_node = current_node.next (or we'd lose the rest of the list), flip the arrow with current_node.next = previous_node, then move both names one node forward. When current_node becomes None, previous_node is the head of the reversed half.
  5. Step 3, weave. first walks the first half and second walks the reversed second half. Each round we save both "next" nodes first, then link first → second → first_next, and step both names forward.
  6. The loop stops when second runs out. The first half is the same length or one node longer, and its last node already ends with None because of the cut.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 2, head = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5] (expected [1, 5, 2, 4, 3]).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 457. Circular Array Loop Array

Problem: From index i you jump nums[i] steps (wrapping around). Is there a cycle of length > 1 where every jump goes the same direction?

Spot it: "circular" + "jump by nums[i]" defines a next function (i + nums[i]) % n. Detect a cycle with fast/slow, with extra rules.

Key insight: abort a run as soon as fast would step onto a node of the opposite direction or a self-loop (next(j) == j). Afterwards, zero out the path you walked so each index is explored once overall: O(n).

Approach:

  1. For each unvisited start i, remember its direction (forward if nums[i] > 0).
  2. Run slow/fast with next(i) = (i + nums[i]) % n, but only while fast's next two steps keep that direction and aren't self-loops.
  3. If slow == fast, a valid cycle exists → True.
  4. Otherwise zero out every index on this same-direction path so it's never explored again.
  5. If no start finds a cycle, return False.
class Solution:
    def next_index(self, nums: List[int], index: int) -> int:
        # Jump nums[index] steps. "% size" wraps around the circle;
        # in Python the result of % is always between 0 and size - 1,
        # even when the jump is negative.
        size = len(nums)
        return (index + nums[index]) % size

    def is_legal_step(self, nums: List[int], index: int, forward: bool) -> bool:
        # 1) 0 means "already explored, leads nowhere": not legal.
        if nums[index] == 0:
            return False
        # 2) It must move in the same direction as the run we started.
        moves_forward = nums[index] > 0
        if moves_forward != forward:
            return False
        # 3) Jumping back onto itself is a loop of length 1: not allowed.
        if self.next_index(nums, index) == index:
            return False
        return True

    def circularArrayLoop(self, nums: List[int]) -> bool:
        size = len(nums)
        for start in range(size):
            # Skip positions an earlier run already proved useless.
            if nums[start] == 0:
                continue
            # Remember this run's direction (True = forward, False = backward).
            forward = nums[start] > 0

            # Floyd: slow makes 1 jump per round, fast makes 2 jumps.
            slow = start
            fast = start
            while True:
                # fast may only jump if its current spot is legal ...
                if not self.is_legal_step(nums, fast, forward):
                    break
                fast_after_one_jump = self.next_index(nums, fast)
                # ... and the spot after its first jump is legal too.
                if not self.is_legal_step(nums, fast_after_one_jump, forward):
                    break
                slow = self.next_index(nums, slow)
                fast = self.next_index(nums, fast_after_one_jump)
                if slow == fast:
                    return True                   # met inside a valid loop

            # No loop from this start. Zero out the same-direction path we walked
            # so that no later start walks it again (this keeps the total O(n)).
            index = start
            while nums[index] != 0:
                moves_forward = nums[index] > 0
                if moves_forward != forward:
                    break                         # the path turned around: stop
                following = self.next_index(nums, index)   # compute BEFORE zeroing
                nums[index] = 0
                index = following
        return False

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. next_index(nums, index) is the "next pointer": jump nums[index] steps and wrap around with % size. In Python, % always gives a number from 0 to size - 1, even for negative jumps (for example -1 % 5 is 4).
  2. is_legal_step(nums, index, forward) answers "may a valid loop pass through this index?" in three checks: it is not already zeroed out, it moves in the same direction as this run (moves_forward != forward means it would turn around), and it does not jump onto itself (a loop of length 1 is not allowed).
  3. The main for start in range(size): tries every index as a starting point and skips indices that are already 0. forward = nums[start] > 0 records this run's direction.
  4. The while True: loop is Floyd's race with extra rules. Before fast jumps, both the spot it stands on and the spot after its first jump must be legal. If either isn't, break ends this run. Otherwise slow makes one jump, fast makes two (fast_after_one_jump, then one more), and if slow == fast: return True, because only legal steps were taken, so this is a valid loop.
  5. If the run ended without a meeting, the second while loop walks the same path again and sets each same-direction index to 0. We compute following before zeroing, because next_index needs the old value. Zeroing means "dead end, never explore again", which keeps the total work O(n).
  6. If no start finds a loop, return False.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 1, nums = [2, -1, 1, 2, 2] (expected True: the loop 0 → 2 → 3 → 0 only moves forward).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space (it modifies the input as a visited marker).

Easy 141. Linked List Cycle Linked List

Problem: Does the linked list contain a cycle?

Spot it: the warm-up. Template B; the follow-up "O(1) memory" rules out the visited-set solution.

Approach:

  1. Start both runners at the head: slow = head and fast = head.
  2. While fast and fast.next exist: slow takes 1 step, fast takes 2.
  3. If they become the same node, there's a cycle.
  4. If fast falls off the end, there isn't.
class Solution:
    def hasCycle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
        # Both runners start at the head.
        slow = head
        fast = head
        # fast needs two valid nodes ahead of it to take its 2 steps.
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next                      # 1 step
            fast = fast.next.next                 # 2 steps
            if slow is fast:
                return True                       # same NODE: fast lapped slow
        return False                              # fast reached the end: no loop

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. slow = head, fast = head: both runners start at the head.
  2. while fast is not None and fast.next is not None: continue only while the hare has two nodes in front of it. An empty list makes this false right away.
  3. slow = slow.next takes 1 step; fast = fast.next.next takes 2 steps.
  4. if slow is fast: return True: checked after moving (at the start they are trivially equal). Being on the same node means the hare came around the loop and caught up.
  5. return False: the loop ended because the hare reached the end of the list, and a list with an end has no cycle.

8. Common mistakes

Null-pointer crashCalling fast.next.next without checking fast and fast.next first. Always guard with while fast and fast.next.
Checking for a meeting before movingBoth start at head, so slow is fast is true immediately. Move first, then compare.
Comparing values instead of nodesTwo different nodes can hold the same value. Use is (identity) for linked lists.
Wrong middle for the jobwhile fast and fast.next gives the second middle (good for "return the middle"). while fast.next and fast.next.next gives the first middle (good for splitting into halves).
Starting phase 2 at different speedsIn phase 2 both pointers move one step at a time.

9. Self-check quiz

A list has no cycle. When fast can no longer move, where is slow?

Fast walked twice as far as slow. When fast reaches the end, slow has covered half the distance.

Slow and fast just met inside a cycle. How do you find where the cycle begins?

From the math a = kL − b: the head and the meeting point are the same distance from the entrance.

Find the repeated number in [3,1,3,4,2] (values in 1..n) without modifying it, O(1) space.

Sorting modifies the array and a set uses O(n) space. Treating values as next-pointers makes the duplicate the entrance of a cycle.

Once slow enters the cycle, how soon is it guaranteed that fast catches it?

The gap closes by exactly 1 each round and starts below the loop length L, so they meet in fewer than L rounds.

Easy 876. Middle of the Linked List Linked List

Problem: Return the middle node of a linked list (the second middle when the length is even).

Spot it: "Middle" + singly linked list → template A.

Approach:

  1. Start both runners at the head: slow = head and fast = head.
  2. While fast and fast.next: slow takes 1 step, fast takes 2.
  3. Return slow.
class Solution:
    def middleNode(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Both runners start at the head.
        slow = head
        fast = head
        # Keep going while fast can still take 2 steps.
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next                      # 1 step
            fast = fast.next.next                 # 2 steps
        # fast is at (or just past) the end, so slow is in the middle.
        # For an even length this is the SECOND of the two middle nodes.
        return slow

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. slow = head, fast = head: both runners start at the head.
  2. while fast is not None and fast.next is not None: keep going while the hare can take two steps.
  3. slow = slow.next (1 step), fast = fast.next.next (2 steps).
  4. return slow: the hare is at the last node (odd length) or just past it (None, even length). Having walked half as far, the tortoise is in the middle. For an even length that is the second of the two middle nodes, which is what LeetCode wants.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 2, head = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] (expected the node 4).

RoundslowfastCan fast take 2 more steps?
start11yes
123yes
235yes
34Noneno → stop, return slow

The function returns the node 4 (so the answer list is [4, 5, 6]).

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Easy 202. Happy Number MathHash Set

Problem: Keep replacing n with the sum of the squares of its digits. If you reach 1, n is happy; otherwise the numbers loop forever. Is n happy?

Spot it: "Loops forever" + a well-defined next value → cycle detection on numbers instead of nodes.

Approach:

  1. Define sum_of_digit_squares(x) = sum of the squared digits of x (the "next pointer").
  2. slow = n, fast = sum_of_digit_squares(n).
  3. Advance slow by 1 and fast by 2 until fast == 1 or slow == fast.
  4. Happy exactly when fast == 1.
class Solution:
    def sum_of_digit_squares(self, number: int) -> int:
        # This is the implicit "next pointer": 19 -> 1*1 + 9*9 = 82.
        total = 0
        while number > 0:
            digit = number % 10                   # the last digit
            total = total + digit * digit         # add its square
            number = number // 10                 # chop the last digit off
        return total

    def isHappy(self, n: int) -> bool:
        # slow starts at n; fast starts one step ahead so the loop can run.
        slow = n
        fast = self.sum_of_digit_squares(n)
        # Stop when fast reaches 1 (happy) or catches slow (stuck in a loop).
        while fast != 1 and slow != fast:
            slow = self.sum_of_digit_squares(slow)    # slow: 1 step
            fast = self.sum_of_digit_squares(fast)    # fast: first step
            fast = self.sum_of_digit_squares(fast)    # fast: second step
        # Happy exactly when the chain reached 1.
        return fast == 1

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. sum_of_digit_squares(number) is the "next pointer". number % 10 gives the last digit, we add its square to total, and number // 10 (whole-number division) chops that digit off. When number reaches 0, every digit has been used.
  2. In isHappy, slow = n and fast = sum_of_digit_squares(n): fast starts one step ahead so that slow != fast is true and the loop can begin.
  3. while fast != 1 and slow != fast: stop when fast reaches 1 (happy, and 1 maps to itself forever) or when fast catches slow (we are stuck in a loop that doesn't contain 1).
  4. Inside: slow takes one step, fast takes two steps (two separate calls, one per line).
  5. return fast == 1: True if we stopped because we reached 1, False if we stopped because the runners met.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 1, n = 19 (expected True). First, one call of the helper, sum_of_digit_squares(19):

numberdigit = number % 10totalnumber // 10
199811
11820

The helper returns 82. Now the race in isHappy(19):

RoundslowfastSteps taken
start1982fast = sum_of_digit_squares(19) = 82
182100slow: 19 → 82; fast: 82 → 68 → 100
2681slow: 82 → 68; fast: 100 → 1 → 1

fast reached 1, so the function returns True.

Complexity: Each step is O(log n) digits, and the sequence quickly drops below a few hundred, so the time is effectively O(log n). O(1) space.

Medium 2095. Delete the Middle Node of a Linked List Linked List

Problem: Delete the node at index ⌊n/2⌋ and return the head.

Spot it: To unlink a node you need the node before it. Use fast & slow, but give fast a one-round head start so slow stops one node early.

Approach:

  1. If there's only one node, return None.
  2. slow = head, fast = head.next.next (fast starts two steps ahead).
  3. While fast and fast.next: slow takes 1 step, fast takes 2.
  4. slow is now just before the middle: slow.next = slow.next.next.
class Solution:
    def deleteMiddle(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # A single node IS the middle; deleting it leaves an empty list.
        if head.next is None:
            return None
        # Give fast a head start of one round (2 nodes).
        # Then slow stops on the node just BEFORE the middle.
        slow = head
        fast = head.next.next
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next
        # Unlink the middle: slow now points past it.
        middle = slow.next
        slow.next = middle.next
        return head

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if head.next is None: return None: with a single node, that node is the middle; deleting it leaves an empty list.
  2. slow = head, fast = head.next.next: fast gets a one-round head start (two nodes). That shifts where slow stops by one node, so slow ends on the node just before the middle, which is the node we need in order to unlink the middle. (head.next.next is safe: we know head.next exists; it may be None, which the loop handles.)
  3. The usual loop: while fast is not None and fast.next is not None: slow 1 step, fast 2 steps.
  4. middle = slow.next names the node to delete, and slow.next = middle.next makes the list skip over it.
  5. return head: the head itself never changes (the list has at least 2 nodes here).

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 1, head = [1, 3, 4, 7, 1, 2, 6] (n = 7, so delete index 3, the node 7). The value 1 appears twice, so each node also shows its position.

RoundslowfastNote
start1 (node #1)4 (node #3)fast starts two nodes ahead
13 (node #2)1 (node #5)slow 1 step, fast 2 steps
24 (node #3)6 (node #7)slow 1 step, fast 2 steps; fast cannot take 2 more steps → stop
unlink4 (node #3)6 (node #7)middle = 7 (node #4); slow.next = 1 (node #5); list: 1 → 3 → 4 → 1 → 2 → 6

The function returns 1 → 3 → 4 → 1 → 2 → 6.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 234. Palindrome Linked List (O(1) space) Linked List

Problem: Do the list's values read the same forwards and backwards? Follow-up: use O(1) extra space.

Spot it: You need to compare the first half with the second half read backwards → find the middle with fast/slow, then reverse half (pattern 05).

Approach:

  1. Fast/slow: slow lands on the first node of the second half.
  2. Reverse the list from slow onward.
  3. Walk from head and from the reversed half together until the reversed half ends.
  4. Any mismatch → False; otherwise True.
class Solution:
    def isPalindrome(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> bool:
        # Step 1: slow walks to the first node of the second half.
        slow = head
        fast = head
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        # Step 2: reverse the list from slow to the end.
        previous_node = None
        current_node = slow
        while current_node is not None:
            next_node = current_node.next         # remember the rest
            current_node.next = previous_node     # flip the arrow
            previous_node = current_node          # move both forward
            current_node = next_node
        # previous_node is now the head of the reversed second half.

        # Step 3: compare the first half with the reversed second half.
        left = head
        right = previous_node
        while right is not None:                  # the second half is never longer
            if left.val != right.val:
                return False                      # a mismatch: not a palindrome
            left = left.next
            right = right.next
        return True

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Step 1: the usual fast/slow loop (while fast is not None and fast.next is not None) leaves slow on the first node of the second half (the second middle).
  2. Step 2: reverse the list from slow to the end. Each round saves next_node, flips current_node.next to point backwards, and moves previous_node and current_node one node forward. Afterwards previous_node is the head of the reversed second half.
  3. Step 3: left starts at head and right at the reversed half. While right is not None, compare left.val with right.val. Any difference means return False; otherwise move both one node.
  4. return True: every pair matched. We loop on right because the second half is never longer than the first.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 1, head = [1, 2, 2, 1] (expected True). Values repeat, so each node also shows its position.

StageVariablesWhat happened
1 middleslow = 1 (node #1), fast = 1 (node #1)start
1 middleslow = 2 (node #2), fast = 2 (node #3)slow 1 step, fast 2 steps
1 middleslow = 2 (node #3), fast = Noneslow 1 step, fast 2 steps
2 reverseprevious_node = 2 (node #3), current_node = 1 (node #4)reversed half so far: 2
2 reverseprevious_node = 1 (node #4), current_node = Nonereversed half so far: 1 → 2
3 compareleft = 1 (node #1), right = 1 (node #4)equal → move both
3 compareleft = 2 (node #2), right = 2 (node #3)equal → move both
3 compareleft = 2 (node #3), right = Noneright half used up → return True

The function returns True.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space. (It leaves the second half reversed; reverse it back if the caller cares.)

Medium 148. Sort List Linked List

Problem: Sort a linked list in O(n log n) time.

Spot it: Merge sort suits linked lists because it never needs random access; fast/slow finds the split point.

Approach:

  1. Base case: 0 or 1 node is already sorted.
  2. slow = head, fast = head.next; advance until fast ends. slow is now the end of the first half.
  3. Cut after slow and sort both halves recursively.
  4. Merge the two sorted halves (helper merge_two_sorted_lists) using a dummy node and a tail pointer.
class Solution:
    def sortList(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # Base case: 0 or 1 node is already sorted.
        if head is None or head.next is None:
            return head

        # Find the END of the first half. fast starts one node ahead,
        # which makes slow stop on the last node of the first half.
        slow = head
        fast = head.next
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        # Cut the list into two halves.
        second_half = slow.next
        slow.next = None

        # Sort each half (recursion), then merge the two sorted halves.
        sorted_first = self.sortList(head)
        sorted_second = self.sortList(second_half)
        return self.merge_two_sorted_lists(sorted_first, sorted_second)

    def merge_two_sorted_lists(self, left: Optional[ListNode], right: Optional[ListNode]) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # A dummy node in front means we never special-case the first node.
        dummy = ListNode()
        tail = dummy                              # tail = last node of the merged list
        while left is not None and right is not None:
            # Take the smaller front node and attach it after tail.
            if left.val <= right.val:
                tail.next = left
                left = left.next
            else:
                tail.next = right
                right = right.next
            tail = tail.next
        # One list ran out; attach whatever is left of the other one.
        if left is not None:
            tail.next = left
        else:
            tail.next = right
        return dummy.next

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. if head is None or head.next is None: return head: the base case. A list of 0 or 1 nodes is already sorted, and it is what stops the recursion.
  2. slow = head, fast = head.next: fast starts one node ahead, so when the loop ends slow is on the last node of the first half. (If both started at head, a 2-node list would never shrink and the recursion would never end.)
  3. second_half = slow.next then slow.next = None cuts the list into two separate halves.
  4. sorted_first = self.sortList(head) and sorted_second = self.sortList(second_half): recursion. Trust that each call returns its half sorted.
  5. merge_two_sorted_lists(left, right): a dummy node sits in front of the answer so the first real node needs no special case; tail is the last node of the merged list so far. Each round attaches the smaller of the two front nodes after tail and moves that list forward. (<= keeps equal values in their original order.)
  6. When one list runs out, the if left is not None ... else ... attaches the rest of the other list in one go, because it is already sorted. return dummy.next skips the dummy.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 1, head = [4, 2, 1, 3] (expected [1, 2, 3, 4]). Each row is one event in the order it happens; depth 0 is the first call.

Recursion depthEventLists
0split4 → 2 → 1 → 3 ⇒ 4 → 2 | 1 → 3 (slow stopped on 2)
1split4 → 2 ⇒ 4 | 2 (slow stopped on 4)
2base case4 is already sorted
2base case2 is already sorted
1merge4 + 2 = 2 → 4
1split1 → 3 ⇒ 1 | 3 (slow stopped on 1)
2base case1 is already sorted
2base case3 is already sorted
1merge1 + 3 = 1 → 3
0merge2 → 4 + 1 → 3 = 1 → 2 → 3 → 4

The function returns 1 → 2 → 3 → 4.

Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(log n) recursion stack.

Medium 2130. Maximum Twin Sum of a Linked List Linked List

Problem: In a list of even length n, node i and node n−1−i are twins. Return the largest twin sum.

Spot it: Pair the first half with the second half read backwards → middle (fast/slow) + reverse the second half.

Approach:

  1. Fast/slow: slow lands on the first node of the second half.
  2. Reverse the second half.
  3. Walk from head and from the reversed half together, adding twin values.
  4. Return the maximum sum.
class Solution:
    def pairSum(self, head: Optional[ListNode]) -> int:
        # Step 1: slow walks to the first node of the second half.
        slow = head
        fast = head
        while fast is not None and fast.next is not None:
            slow = slow.next
            fast = fast.next.next

        # Step 2: reverse the second half.
        previous_node = None
        current_node = slow
        while current_node is not None:
            next_node = current_node.next         # remember the rest
            current_node.next = previous_node     # flip the arrow
            previous_node = current_node          # move both forward
            current_node = next_node

        # Step 3: left walks forward from the head, right walks forward through
        # the reversed half, which means "backwards" through the original list.
        best_sum = 0
        left = head
        right = previous_node
        while right is not None:
            twin_sum = left.val + right.val
            if twin_sum > best_sum:
                best_sum = twin_sum               # a new best pair
            left = left.next
            right = right.next
        return best_sum

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Step 1: the usual fast/slow loop leaves slow on the first node of the second half (the length is even, so this is node n/2).
  2. Step 2: reverse the second half with previous_node / current_node / next_node, exactly like in 234. previous_node ends on the old last node.
  3. Step 3: left walks forward from the head while right walks the reversed half, which visits the original list from the back. So left and right are always twins.
  4. twin_sum = left.val + right.val; if twin_sum > best_sum: best_sum = twin_sum keeps the largest sum seen so far (all values are positive, so starting from 0 is safe).
  5. return best_sum once the reversed half is used up.

Dry run on the example: LeetCode example 1, head = [5, 4, 2, 1] (expected 6).

StageVariablesWhat happened
1 middleslow = 5, fast = 5start
1 middleslow = 4, fast = 2slow 1 step, fast 2 steps
1 middleslow = 2, fast = Noneslow 1 step, fast 2 steps
2 reverseprevious_node = 2, current_node = 1reversed half so far: 2
2 reverseprevious_node = 1, current_node = Nonereversed half so far: 1 → 2
3 twin sumsleft = 5, right = 1twin_sum = 5 + 1 = 6 → new best_sum = 6
3 twin sumsleft = 4, right = 2twin_sum = 4 + 2 = 6 → best_sum stays 6
3 twin sumsright = Noneloop ends → return 6

The function returns 6.

Complexity: O(n) time, O(1) space.

Medium 19. Remove Nth Node From End of List Linked List

Problem: Remove the n-th node from the end of the linked list and return its head, in one pass.

Spot it: "N-th from the end" without knowing the length → two runners. Here they move at the same speed but with a head start of n, so when the leader falls off the end, the follower stands just before the target.

Key insight: A dummy node before head means the node before the target always exists, even when the target is the head itself (n equal to the length).

Approach:

  1. Put a dummy node in front of head.
  2. Move fast forward n nodes from head.
  3. Start slow at dummy, then move both one step at a time until fast is None.
  4. slow is now just before the node to delete: set slow.next = slow.next.next.
  5. Return dummy.next (the head may have changed).
class Solution:
    def removeNthFromEnd(self, head: Optional[ListNode], n: int) -> Optional[ListNode]:
        # a fake node before head, so removing the head needs no special case
        dummy = ListNode(0, head)
        fast = head
        # give fast a head start of n nodes
        for _ in range(n):
            fast = fast.next
        slow = dummy
        # move together; the gap between them stays n
        while fast is not None:
            fast = fast.next
            slow = slow.next
        # slow is right before the node to remove: skip over it
        slow.next = slow.next.next
        return dummy.next

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. dummy = ListNode(0, head): a placeholder whose next is the real head.
  2. for _ in range(n): fast = fast.next: fast walks n nodes ahead. (_ means we don't need the loop counter.)
  3. slow = dummy: slow starts one node before the head. That extra step is what leaves it in front of the target, not on it.
  4. while fast is not None: move both one step per round; the gap of n + 1 positions between them never changes.
  5. When fast is None (just past the last node), slow is n + 1 positions back: the node before the target.
  6. slow.next = slow.next.next: unlink the target. return dummy.next handles the case where the old head was removed.

Dry run on the example:

head = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5], n = 2 (LeetCode Example 1). Returns [1, 2, 3, 5].

phasefastslownote
head start3—fast moved 2 nodes: 1 → 2 → 3
start3dummymove together
round 141
round 252
round 3None3fast fell off: stop
unlink33.next = 5, node 4 is gone → [1, 2, 3, 5]

Complexity: O(L) time (one pass over the list), O(1) space.
